explain.say: An SSD has no moving parts. It stores data in billions of tiny flash memory cells, each a special transistor that can trap electrons and hold them even with the power off.

explain.say: To write, a high voltage on the control gate pulls electrons up from the silicon channel through a very thin insulating layer. They get stuck on the floating gate, sealed in by insulation all around.

explain.say: To read, the SSD checks whether current flows through the channel. Trapped electrons make the cell harder to switch on, so the controller can tell a charged cell from an empty one, a 0 from a 1.

explain.say: Squeezing electrons through the oxide slowly damages it, so each cell survives only thousands of rewrites. The SSD spreads writing evenly across all its cells, called wear levelling, so the drive lasts for years.

faq.q: How does a floating gate store a bit?
faq.a: The floating gate is a tiny island of conductor surrounded completely by insulation. Electrons pushed onto it cannot escape, so the cell stays charged or empty for years without power, and that state is the bit.
asks: How does flash memory keep data without power?

faq.q: What does the control gate do?
faq.a: The control gate sits on top of the cell. A high voltage on it pulls electrons onto the floating gate to write, and a smaller voltage is used to test the cell when reading.
asks: How is data written to an SSD?

faq.q: How does an SSD read a bit?
faq.a: The controller puts a test voltage on the control gate and checks whether current flows through the silicon channel. An empty cell switches on easily; a charged cell does not. Many SSDs store 3 or 4 bits per cell by measuring how much charge is trapped.

Each write and erase forces electrons through the thin tunnel oxide, which slowly damages it until the cell can no longer hold charge. The controller spreads writes across all cells and keeps spare ones, so a normal drive lasts many years.

faq.q: Why are SSDs faster than hard drives?
faq.a: An SSD reads data electronically in about a tenth of a millisecond, while a hard drive must spin its disc and swing its arm to the right spot, taking around 10 milliseconds. An SSD also reads many chips at once.
asks: SSD or hard drive, which is faster?

facts: In NAND flash, an erased cell with no trapped charge reads as 1.
Triple-level cell (TLC) flash stores 3 bits in each cell by using 8 different amounts of trapped charge.
Many modern SSDs trap charge in an insulating layer (charge-trap flash) instead of a floating gate, but the idea is the same.
